episodes.title: Likeability Expert: Stop Doing This, It’s Why People Quietly Avoid You! | Vanessa Van Edwards
episodes.summary: 20 points taken verbatim from The Diary Of A CEO, spanning 6:54–2:17:07. Selected from the transcript by information density — every line below is what was said, not a description of it.

learnings.headline: Accidentally, I've been doing research for this my whole life because I was very bad at…
learnings.detail: So accidentally, I've been doing research for this my whole life because I was very bad at conversation for 20 years.
learnings.passage: And that's a very different way of thinking about, oh, I want to impress somebody. So how long have you spent doing the research that feeds into what we're going to talk about today and feeds into this new book? Okay. So accidentally, I've been doing research for this my whole life because I was very bad at conversation for 20 years. Then 20 years ago, I realized that there are these hidden blueprints behind our interactions. I wasn't quite sure what they were, but I could see that very good conversationalists, they were following some kind of plan. Okay. Then eight years ago, this is when the real research began, and it started with an experiment. I call it my speed networking experiment. This fundamentally changed the way I think about conversations. Here's what we did.
learnings.evidence: So accidentally, I've been doing research for this my whole life because I was very bad at conversation for 20 years.

learnings.headline: It's very hard for someone to break out of that fact because they're stuck in that…
learnings.detail: So it's very hard for someone to break out of that fact because they're stuck in that social script.
learnings.passage: That was the fifth worst. Very close to the bottom. Sixth was? Something about the weather. What do you do? What do you do? That was the worst. The worst. Okay. Why? So these last two, how are you and what do you do? They're very socially scripted, right? The moment we ask those questions, our brain goes into autopilot. So there's a lack. It is more of a performance. There's a lack of excitement in the conversation. And they ran out of things to talk about. They're fact-based questions. And this is the trap of what we'll call level one conversation, which is you are trapped in fact. Where are you from? Got any kids? Married? The facts are dead ends, right? So it's very hard for someone to break out of that fact because they're stuck in that social script.
learnings.evidence: So it's very hard for someone to break out of that fact because they're stuck in that social script.

learnings.headline: The reason why this one is important, and I agonized over this third question because…
learnings.detail: Now, the reason why this one is important, and I agonized over this third question because there's three questions for each level, is have any fun plans coming up is a subtle way to bring up potential shared future.
learnings.passage: And actually saying and using in conversation these phrases is... is a way that we can create more intrigue and interest. And I know that sounds like, what? But think about this. If something crazy happened to you yesterday and you walk into dinner and you're like, guys, the craziest thing happened to me yesterday, everyone's like, phone's down. Right? Now, I couldn't say something boring. I couldn't be like, I was stuck in traffic. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Unless you want to be funny. But I think that looking for opportunities to create that little bit of conversational confetti, they come up with questions like this. And this is the last one. Have any fun plans coming up? Now, the reason why this one is important, and I agonized over this third question because there's three questions for each level, is have any fun plans coming up is a subtle way to bring up potential shared future.
learnings.evidence: Now, the reason why this one is important, and I agonized over this third question because there's three questions for each level, is have any fun plans coming up is a subtle way to bring up potential shared future.

learnings.headline: The mistake traps people make is they skip level one.
learnings.detail: So the mistake traps people make is they skip level one.
learnings.passage: Exactly. So this is us going deeper with the person. Exactly. Or leveling up as you wish. Right. As you wish. So the mistake traps people make is they skip level one. They try to go too deep quickly and people feel like it's invasive. Right. Especially when you're like, whoa, slow down or can feel like an interrogation. So we must know those basics first as long as we do them better. We don't do them in autopilot way. Level two is when you start to understand what motivates someone. The kind of mental trick that I use is you know you're on level two with someone if you know what gets them up in the morning, like what goal is driving them all day. But you also know what keeps them up at night, what worries them. I encourage people as they're reading, like think of the five people you interact with most and place them on a level.
learnings.evidence: So the mistake traps people make is they skip level one.

learnings.headline: What have you always wanted to learn is an interesting question because it triggers…
learnings.detail: Okay, so what have you always wanted to learn is an interesting question because it triggers growth mindset.
learnings.passage: But pet projects, the things they love, have a lot of pride. And so you're trying to figure out in conversation, could you let someone feel safe enough to share either one? And are there questions that evoke dream building? Yes. Okay, so what have you always wanted to learn is an interesting question because it triggers growth mindset. right? So growth mindset is when someone believes they can change themselves, change who they are, change their trajectory, learn something new. So we like this question because you're asking, are you willing to grow with me? What have you always wanted to learn? The other easy one is, what is your biggest goal right now? So what is your biggest goal right now is a great question.
learnings.evidence: Okay, so what have you always wanted to learn is an interesting question because it triggers growth mindset.

learnings.headline: I was researching this book, and I was eavesdropping on everyone's conversations,…
learnings.detail: I was researching this book, and I was eavesdropping on everyone's conversations, because that's the best way.
learnings.passage: And we don't want to overcomplicate or be vague. So, for example, I was sitting in a coffee shop. I was researching this book, and I was eavesdropping on everyone's conversations, because that's the best way. You know, if you listen to conversations in the wild, all the things you hear are great. And I was on my computer, and I heard – she said, so, what do you do? I think they were on, like, a date. And he goes, oh, I have a system for maximizing achievement in young learners. Right? And she was like, what? And he goes, yeah, I work with fifth grade students and I have a system for how they can learn math and reading. And she goes, oh, you're a teacher. He goes, yeah, I'm a fifth grade teacher. And I was like, wow.
learnings.evidence: I was researching this book, and I was eavesdropping on everyone's conversations, because that's the best way.

learnings.headline: First is let's do an intervention on this is go back if you have recorded Zoom calls…
learnings.detail: First is let's do an intervention on this is go back if you have recorded Zoom calls and just time yourself.
learnings.passage: And 71% of respondents said talkative co-workers prevented them from getting their work done. Yes. How does one know if they are the person that talks too much? First is let's do an intervention on this is go back if you have recorded Zoom calls and just time yourself. There is a kind of appropriate, right, 15 to 45 seconds, 45 seconds is the most. Second, nonverbal cues. Someone is checking out if they are opening their mouth as if to say something. That is a subtle cue that someone wants to turn, but they are going to wait. So if someone is opening their mouth, I call it the open fish, okay? It means they want to turn. Like, you did it to me earlier, and I totally stopped. Yeah, you did, yeah.
learnings.evidence: First is let's do an intervention on this is go back if you have recorded Zoom calls and just time yourself.

learnings.detail: Like if this is the person you're going to invest in and you care for and you like, you have to you have to stand up for what you want to share.
learnings.passage: Do you want to hear about mine? Do you want to hear about my goal? Right. In your experience, where does that conversational narcissism come from? Insecurity. Yeah. Right. This person's insecure. I don't even know them. They're insecure. And also, my bet is they're trying to impress you. My bet is they're trying to find something to raise your eyebrows. But they don't realize that the more they talk, the more you're like, can I go home? Do you think they know that they're a conversational narcissist? Do you think they're listening right now and think, fuck, that's me?
learnings.evidence: Like if this is the person you're going to invest in and you care for and you like, you have to you have to stand up for what you want to share.

learnings.headline: Meaning, if you want to be likable, you have to go around assertively and aggressively…
learnings.detail: Meaning, if you want to be likable, you have to go around assertively and aggressively liking as many people as possible.
learnings.passage: The most popular kids were the kids who had the longest list of people they liked. Yeah. Meaning, if you want to be likable, you have to go around assertively and aggressively liking as many people as possible. Because if you go into conversations thinking, how could I like you? How could I like you? How could I like you more? It's less about you. And you're asking questions that are setting them up to be likable. I wonder, and I wish I could take a crack at this conversational narcissist that you know, but... If I were to ask more questions of them, like really set them up to entertain me, to get deep, to actually let them go to level two and maybe even level three if they want to, would they calm down?
learnings.evidence: Meaning, if you want to be likable, you have to go around assertively and aggressively liking as many people as possible.

learnings.headline: Just generally like if it's an idea, everything in my head is a story first.
learnings.detail: Just generally like if it's an idea, everything in my head is a story first.
learnings.passage: Ooh, a yap challenge. A yap challenge is you open up your phone camera and you teach something or share an opinion about something without notes. And you hit record. If you go naturally 15 or 30 seconds, you're probably good. If you're hitting 45 seconds, that's the max. If you're up to a minute or two minutes, you probably talk too much. Hmm. About yourself or just about yourself, but like that, that your typical answering length is longer than conversationally appropriate to a question about you. A yap challenge could be share your opinion about veganism. Damn. I didn't think I could get that done in 15 seconds. What's your answer? No, not to veganism. Just generally like if it's an idea, everything in my head is a story first.
learnings.evidence: Just generally like if it's an idea, everything in my head is a story first.

learnings.headline: I think a mistake that people make is they are afraid of going too deep too quickly,…
learnings.detail: I think a mistake that people make is they are afraid of going too deep too quickly, and they're afraid of going deep in conversation because it feels scary to be vulnerable.
learnings.passage: So we have to use dating apps. I think they're the only way that we'll be able to connect. So I'm actually, I'm pro dating app. Of course, I would love for people to approach in person, but I'm not pro not talking first. And I think if someone asks for your handle, you're fair to say, it's just for my friends and family. Let's try to get there. Okay, I concede. No, I think it makes sense. It doesn't make sense. Okay, we did it. It's hard to repeat. Okay, so this is a wonderful level, but it's reserved for your most important people. I think a mistake that people make is they are afraid of going too deep too quickly, and they're afraid of going deep in conversation because it feels scary to be vulnerable.
learnings.evidence: I think a mistake that people make is they are afraid of going too deep too quickly, and they're afraid of going deep in conversation because it feels scary to be vulnerable.

learnings.headline: When you have a contamination narrative or you're in a relationship with someone with a…
learnings.detail: When you have a contamination narrative or you're in a relationship with someone with a contamination narrative, the only way that I think we can change that, because our narratives are changeable, these are not fixed personality traits, is via conversation.
learnings.passage: The other kind of narrative is a contamination narrative. People with a contamination narrative... They feel that all the hardship and all the challenge and all the struggle has happened to them and they can't make it through. They can't overcome. That no matter how hard they've worked their grit, their strength, their resilience, they're a victim of circumstance. They typically feel very unlucky and very out of control. And when you have that kind of narrative, it's less about the facts of your life and more about the frames of your life, how you're seeing those facts, how you're seeing those facts. When you have a contamination narrative or you're in a relationship with someone with a contamination narrative, the only way that I think we can change that, because our narratives are changeable, these are not fixed personality traits, is via conversation.
learnings.evidence: When you have a contamination narrative or you're in a relationship with someone with a contamination narrative, the only way that I think we can change that, because our narratives are changeable, these are not fixed personality traits, is via conversation.

learnings.headline: The third answer for Lucky Thank You is that person who is afraid to answer.
learnings.detail: Okay, so the third answer for Lucky Thank You is that person who is afraid to answer.
learnings.passage: If you know their luck, you're going to be able to predict behavior. A lot of how they are in a relationship, how they are as a friend, how they are going to be at work. Right? Fate, I think, is an interesting one to ask someone. And then there's other questions that seem silly but actually have tremendous meaning. And level three is all about meaning. Okay, so the third answer for Lucky Thank You is that person who is afraid to answer. And I have asked this question of thousands of people. And you get this bucket of, um, well... Kind of. Now, this is very interesting because this tells you they're probably not that introspective. So it's one of two things. They actually don't know. They literally have not ever thought about it.
learnings.evidence: Okay, so the third answer for Lucky Thank You is that person who is afraid to answer.

learnings.headline: A really critical part of this exercise is that you ask someone about the character and…
learnings.detail: A really critical part of this exercise is that you ask someone about the character and then you say why, what traits, because the traits that they say next are going to tell you every single thing about that person.
learnings.passage: And then he went on to be successful. So it was, it gave me a lot of hope. So, and he's also black. Yeah. So it was really important in that interaction that I didn't assume about that character. I asked you why, and then you told me a story about what you saw and when you saw it. A really critical part of this exercise is that you ask someone about the character and then you say why, what traits, because the traits that they say next are going to tell you every single thing about that person. For example, if I ask someone, you know, what person are you most like? And they say, Mother Teresa. I say, oh, you know, why? You know, I might not agree with them. Maybe I don't see that. But whatever they say next is going to tell me a lot about how they view themselves, whether it's true or not. And this is the hardest part about Level 3, and it's the most inconvenient part of Level 3.
learnings.evidence: A really critical part of this exercise is that you ask someone about the character and then you say why, what traits, because the traits that they say next are going to tell you every single thing about that person.

learnings.headline: The moment they have a baby, they flip into self-help because all of a sudden their…
learnings.detail: The moment they have a baby, they flip into self-help because all of a sudden their purpose is theirs to take care of this little person.
learnings.passage: I've seen this happen with both moms and dads. The moment they have a baby, they flip into self-help because all of a sudden their purpose is theirs to take care of this little person. The problem is that they have a really hard time saying no. That people pleases. Yeah. They struggle with boundaries. They say yes to too much. And they put themselves last. Can be both good and bad in a relationship. And so if you're in a relationship with them, sometimes half of it is just letting them stand up to protect themselves. To not give too much. And I mentioned this very briefly earlier, but I've had many friends who are selfless helpers and they attract takers. They attract high-conflict people. You know what I mean by high-conflict?
learnings.evidence: The moment they have a baby, they flip into self-help because all of a sudden their purpose is theirs to take care of this little person.

learnings.detail: So sometimes they won't take the ball because they're worried it's selfish.
learnings.passage: And so if you're dealing with a selfless helper in terms of conversation. Yes. Sometimes they even think talking about themselves is taking advantage. Okay. So you might sometimes in conversation, like you're asking them a question. They're like, oh, no, no. Enough about me. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Oh, let's talk about you. Yeah. Oh, I want to help you. How can I help you? It's so funny. Like my friends who are selfless helpers, I cannot get them to tell me what I can help them with because all they want to do is check in on me. I'm like, no, no, I really do want to hear about you. So sometimes they won't take the ball because they're worried it's selfish. And so sometimes getting them to open up can be hard because they feel like their needs are not important, but their needs are very important.
learnings.evidence: So sometimes they won't take the ball because they're worried it's selfish.

learnings.headline: You are actually giving away your vocal competence because I'm so far away from my…
learnings.detail: You are actually giving away your vocal competence because I'm so far away from my maximum resonance point.
learnings.passage: Hello. Hello, everyone. Hi. Ooh. You are actually giving away your vocal competence because I'm so far away from my maximum resonance point. My maximum resonance point is when I speak on the out breath. So my vocal cords are relaxed. So now listen to the difference. So here's the hi. Hello. Versus hello. Both me, but you're going to treat me totally differently. So now take a deep breath and say hello on the out breath. Hello. Right. Now, that sounds more like you because you usually use your maximum resonance point. Yeah. Right? You're very good at that. And I've noticed that in work culture, people who use their maximum resonance point, they are listened to more. They are easy to talk to because we want to listen to them.
